1) in the presence of occlusions, the problem is not overdetermined and the local orientation can not be computed from two images alone; 2) in the presence noise, integrability can not be used to resolve the ambiguity; 3) two regularization schemes are proposed to improve numerical performance of the method; and 4) the theory applies to color photometric stereo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a fundamental problem of 3D vision: how to recover surface geometry from images in which the light is occluded by the object itself.
the problem of recovering the shape from a pair of uncalibrated images, where the light source direction is known.

the following questions: How does the geometry of the surface affect the quality of the reconstruction? How can one improve the numerical stability of the reconstruction? And how can one use the theory to reconstruct the geometry of surfaces in color images?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach can recover a good estimate of the surface normal in the shadow regions and that the method is robust to noise.
, in the case of 3 source photometric stereo with light occlusions and noise, our method is the best available method.
, in the absence of light occlusions, the proposed method provides a reliable solution to the problem of shape reconstruction from two images.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can recover the geometry of a scene with two images and no light source occlusions, but only if there is no noise in the images.
the problem is well-posed for a single light source, ill-posed for multiple light sources and can be made well-posed again by using regularization.
we have shown that, even when only two images without occlusions are available, we can still recover the geometry in shadowed areas.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to overcome light occlusions in 3-source color photometric stereo.
it is possible to reconstruct the surface geometry in the presence of occlusions using only two images and a regularization term.
, even in the presence of shadows, photometric stereo can be applied to reconstruct the shape of a scene from a small number of images.
